title: Beware of Metacognitive Laziness: Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Learning Motivation, Processes, and Performance
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different forms of learning support—especially generative AI—affect learners’ motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL) processes, and performance. Framed within the emerging concept of hybrid intelligence, the study asks whether learners benefit differently when supported by ChatGPT, a human expert, writing analytics tools, or no additional tool at all. A central concern is whether generative AI may improve short-term task performance while encouraging over-reliance and reducing learners’ metacognitive engagement, which the authors describe as “metacognitive laziness.”

The intervention was a randomized lab experiment comparing four conditions: (1) ChatGPT 4.0 support, (2) one-on-one chat with a human expert, (3) checklist-style writing analytics tools, and (4) a control condition with no extra support. Participants completed a two-stage English reading, writing, and revision task focused on imagining the future of education in 2035 using source materials on AI, differentiated teaching, and scaffolding. The researchers collected post-task intrinsic motivation survey data, fine-grained learning trace data to model SRL processes, and objective performance outcomes including essay score improvement, knowledge gain, and knowledge transfer.

The sample consisted of 117 university students recruited from July to September 2023. Participants were English second-language speakers and included both undergraduates and graduate students. The study was conducted in a lab setting using a custom digital learning environment with embedded tools for planning, note-taking, dictionary support, and condition-specific supports during the revision stage. A human expert specializing in academic writing participated as an instructional support agent, making educator involvement part of the study context.

The main findings were that intrinsic motivation did not significantly differ across groups, but SRL processes and performance did. The ChatGPT group showed significantly greater essay score improvement than the control, human expert, and checklist groups, suggesting an advantage for short-term writing performance. However, the groups did not differ significantly in knowledge gain or knowledge transfer. Process analyses suggested that learners using ChatGPT relied more heavily on the AI during revision and engaged less in some metacognitive activities than learners supported by a human expert or checklist tools. The authors conclude that while generative AI can boost immediate task performance, it may also foster dependence on AI and weaken deeper self-regulatory engagement, raising concerns for long-term learning in hybrid human-AI educational settings.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on the GPT family, used for conversational assistance and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as revision support during a university English reading-and-writing task. Students in the AI group interacted with ChatGPT through a chat interface embedded in the study platform; it was restricted to task topics and intended to provide advice rather than directly generate the essay.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment with 117 university students, the ChatGPT group showed significantly greater essay score improvement after revision than all other groups. Pairwise differences in improvement favored ChatGPT over control (mean difference=1.970, p-adjusted=0.037), human expert (mean difference=2.120, p-adjusted=0.025), and checklist tools (mean difference=2.200, p-adjusted=0.012); the omnibus test was significant (F=4.549, p=0.005, η2=0.108).
findings.measure: Essay score improvement after revision based on researcher scoring rubric

findings.finding_summary: The ChatGPT group did not differ significantly from the other groups on knowledge gain measured by pre/post scores on the same AI-in-education knowledge test. ANOVA showed no significant group differences for pre-test (F=1.294, p=0.281, η2=0.036) or post-test (F=0.913, p=0.438, η2=0.030).
findings.measure: Knowledge gain on AI-in-education test (pre-test/post-test scores)

findings.finding_summary: The ChatGPT group showed no significant advantage in knowledge transfer relative to the other groups on a transfer test about AI in healthcare. The omnibus test found no group differences (F=0.019, p=0.996, η2=0.000).
findings.measure: Knowledge transfer test score on AI in healthcare

findings.finding_summary: There were no significant differences across groups in post-task intrinsic motivation, including the ChatGPT group. For the IMI subscales, omnibus tests were non-significant: Interest/Enjoyment (F=1.087, p=0.358, η2=0.029), Perceived Competence (F=0.453, p=0.716, η2=0.012), Effort/Importance (F=1.152, p=0.332, η2=0.030), and Pressure/Tension (F=0.546, p=0.652, η2=0.015).
findings.measure: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, effort/importance, pressure/tension)
findings.effect_size: Interest/Enjoyment η2=0.029; Perceived Competence η2=0.012; Effort/Importance η2=0.030; Pressure/Tension η2=0.015

findings.finding_summary: Process analyses indicated that learners using ChatGPT showed different self-regulated learning patterns, with revision activity centered more heavily on interactions with ChatGPT and relatively fewer metacognitive processes such as evaluation and orientation compared with the human expert group. The authors interpret this as evidence that ChatGPT may promote dependence on AI and potential 'metacognitive laziness,' though no single effect size was reported for this process-mining result.
findings.measure: Self-regulated learning processes from trace data, including frequencies and temporal transitions among orientation, planning, monitoring, evaluation, reading, elaboration/organization, and tool interaction

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic GPT-based writing analytics and feedback tools that provide automated writing-related feedback rather than a single clearly named standalone product.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the checklist tools condition: a writing analytics toolkit providing feedback on spelling/grammar, academic style, originality, and rhetorical structure during essay revision.

findings.finding_summary: The checklist-tool condition did not differ significantly from the other groups on post-task intrinsic motivation. Across IMI subscales, omnibus tests were non-significant: Interest/Enjoyment (F=1.087, p=0.358, η2=0.029), Perceived Competence (F=0.453, p=0.716, η2=0.012), Effort/Importance (F=1.152, p=0.332, η2=0.030), and Pressure/Tension (F=0.546, p=0.652, η2=0.015).
findings.measure: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, effort/importance, pressure/tension)
findings.effect_size: Interest/Enjoyment η2=0.029; Perceived Competence η2=0.012; Effort/Importance η2=0.030; Pressure/Tension η2=0.015

findings.finding_summary: The checklist-tool group improved less on essay scores than the ChatGPT group. Pairwise comparison showed the checklist condition was significantly lower than ChatGPT in essay score improvement (mean difference for CL-AI=-2.200, 95% CI [-4.033, -0.367], p-adjusted=0.012); the omnibus test was significant (F=4.549, p=0.005, η2=0.108).
findings.measure: Essay score improvement after revision based on researcher scoring rubric

findings.finding_summary: Learners using the checklist tools showed significantly more evaluation processes during revision than the control group, a pattern the authors attribute to the diagnostic design of the checklist tools that guided learners to use rubrics to evaluate and revise their own writing. No specific effect size or exact test statistic for this between-group process difference was reported in the text.
findings.measure: Self-regulated learning evaluation processes from trace data during revision

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experimental study with multiple comparison groups and n=117, which is stronger than correlational evidence. However, it is a lab-based single-task university study with some limitations and incomplete reporting of some process-analysis statistics, so it falls short of blue-tier rigor.
impact_tier_rationale: The clearest reported effect is for ChatGPT on essay score improvement, with a modest omnibus effect size (η2=0.108) and significant pairwise advantages over all other groups. Most other outcomes were null or qualitatively mixed, so overall impact is modest rather than large.
